cases.reply: In Class E airspace above 10,000 MSL, the VFR cloud clearance requirement is to be "clear of clouds." The rule is in 14 CFR §103.23. The text states: "No person may operate an ultralight vehicle when the flight visibility or distance from clouds is less than that in the table found below. For Class E airspace above 10,000 MSL, the requirement is clear of clouds. The source is 14 CFR §103.23.

To enter Class B airspace as a VFR pilot, you need an explicit ATC clearance — "cleared into the Bravo." You must also have a Mode C transponder, ADS-B Out, and a two-way radio. The full call sign must be read back to the controller. The clearance will include an altitude assignment and may specify a route or heading.

REFERENCE: 
- **FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-1-18, Operational Requests.**
- **AIM 3-4-1, Class B Airspace.**
- **AIM 3-4-2, Class B Airspace — Pilot/Controller Responsibilities.**

Above 3,000 feet AGL and up to 18,000 feet MSL, aircraft must maintain specific flight levels:

- From 3,000 feet to 10,000 feet MSL: Divide the MSL altitude by 100 and round down to the nearest 100 feet. For example, at 3,500 feet AGL, the flight level is 100; at 10,500 feet MSL, the flight level is 100.

- From 10,000 feet to 18,000 feet MSL: Use the same method. For example, at 10,500 feet MSL, the flight level is 100; at 18,000 feet MSL, the flight level is 180.

The rule is in 14 CFR §91.159(a). The text states:

> "Except while holding in a holding pattern of 2 minutes or less, or while turning, each person operating an aircraft under VFR in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface shall maintain the appropriate altitude or flight level prescribed below, unless otherwise authorized by ATC:

> (a) When operating below 18,000 feet MSL and—

> (1) From 3,000 feet to 10,000 feet MSL, the aircraft must maintain an altitude that corresponds to a specific flight level.

> (2) From 10,000 feet to 18,000 feet MSL, the aircraft must maintain an altitude that corresponds to a specific flight level."

Don't know specific scenarios; refer to 14 CFR §91.159(a) for more details.

When two aircraft of the same category are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft to the right has the right-of-way. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.113(d). For different categories, the specific rules for those categories determine the right-of-way.

To ensure the safety of the flight, follow these key preflight actions:

- Assess the operating environment (14 CFR §91.4): Consider local weather, airspace, ground hazards, and surface activity.
- Inform participants (14 CFR §91.4): Brief all participants on operating conditions, emergency procedures, roles, and hazards.
- Ensure proper functioning of control links (14 CFR §91.4): Verify ground control station connections.
- Check power availability (14 CFR §91.4): Ensure sufficient power for the intended flight.
- Secure objects (14 CFR §91.4): Make sure all attached or carried objects are secure.
- Comply with over human beings requirements (14 CFR §107.110 for UAS): Meet the requirements for operations over people.

Always refer to the most current FAA publications for the latest requirements.

Below 18,000 MSL, set your altimeter to the current reported altimeter setting of a station within 100 nautical miles of your route. Use the nearest station if no station is within range. If no station is available, set the altimeter to the elevation of the departure airport or an appropriate setting before departure. The rule is 14 CFR §91.121(a)(1).

Above 10,000 MSL, a Mode C transponder is required per 14 CFR §91.215. Below 10,000 MSL, the requirement does not apply, but Mode A and Mode S transponders are still needed if in Class A, B, or C airspace. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.215. For more, see the AIM's radar equipment and transponder requirements.

The pilot-in-command has final authority over the aircraft. This is stated in 14 CFR §91.3(a): "The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft." In an emergency, the pilot may deviate from any rule in 14 CFR part 91 as needed.

- Altitude assignments
- Heading and vector assignments
- Speed instructions
- Hold-short instructions
- Runway-crossing clearances

The full call sign goes first to ensure the controller matches the readback to the flight. Partial readbacks can lead to misidentification.

Rotate before the jet's rotation point, climb above its track, and stay upwind. The vortices sink and drift, so staying above and upwind helps avoid them. Monitor your altitude; vortices can sink to within 100 to 200 feet. Always be vigilant. Follow AIM 7-4-6 for more details.

An IFR flight requires a filed alternate airport if the primary destination's weather is expected to be at or below the published minimums. Specifically, 14 CFR §91.169 mandates an alternate unless:

- Helicopter operations under Part 97 of the CFR are conducted.
- Weather forecasts show at least 2,000 feet ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility 1 hour before and after the estimated arrival time.

If the weather forecast indicates conditions below the minimums, a filed alternate is required.

Takeoff minimums for Part 91 VFR operations are defined in 14 CFR §91.155, requiring a ceiling of at least 300 feet and visibility of at least 3 miles. For VFR in Class E or higher airspace, the cloud clearance requirements are more stringent, as noted in 14 CFR §91.155(a): 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above, and 1 statute mile horizontal visibility above 10,000 MSL. For IFR operations, you need an IFR flight plan and ATC clearance, with specific takeoff minimums detailed in IAP charts. The rule is 14 CFR §91.173.

On a missed approach, follow these steps:

- Execute the missed approach procedure as specified on the approach plate.
- Climb and turn toward the missed approach point.
- Adhere to the published procedure for obstruction clearance.
- Follow the missed approach if visual reference is lost.
- Request clearance for your intended action.
- Climb to a safe altitude before proceeding.
- Proceed to the holding point or an alternate airport if needed.

Always refer to the specific missed approach procedure on the approach plate and AIM 5-4-21.

The minimum en-route altitude (MEA) for IFR operations is defined in 14 CFR §91.177. It must be at least 1,200 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the centerline of the route. The MEA is published on aeronautical charts and must be followed for the segments of the route as shown. If no MEA is published, use the higher of the minimums specified in 14 CFR §91.177(a) or (b). For more detail, see the MEA section in the AIM or 14 CFR part 91.

A clearance limit in your ATC clearance specifies the farthest point or fix to which you are authorized to fly based on that clearance. It defines the boundary of the clearance you have been given.

- Cleared to the VOR/DME, Victor 10, via the V10A approach.
- Cleared to the intersection of Runway 18L and taxiway A.
- Cleared to the airport of destination.

You are responsible for maintaining your position within the clearance limit. If you need to continue beyond the clearance limit, you will receive another clearance.

- If your clearance is "Cleared to the VOR/DME, Victor 10, via the V10A approach," you are cleared to fly to the VOR/DME and can follow the V10A approach. You would need another clearance to continue beyond this point.

The clearance limit is a critical part of your clearance. Always ensure you understand and comply with the clearance limit to avoid overflying or flying into areas without a clearance.

Continue the flight according to the last ATC clearance received. If no specific route is assigned, follow the route filed in your flight plan. Maintain the highest altitude or flight level as specified in 14 CFR §91.185(c). The rule is in 14 CFR §91.185. Report the radio failure to an appropriate aeronautical facility as soon as possible.

Approach categories are based on an aircraft's stall speed in the landing configuration at maximum gross weight. Categories are:

- **Category A:** Speed < 91 knots.
- **Category B:** 91-120 knots.
- **Category C:** 121-140 knots.
- **Category D:** 141-165 knots.
- **Category E:** ≥ 166 knots.

An aircraft in Category C circling at >121 knots must use Category D minimums. Categories are defined in 14 CFR part 97, guiding approach and landing procedures.

VFR-on-top allows you to operate under Visual Flight Rules at an altitude of your choice, provided you can maintain VFR conditions. You can request it under these conditions:

- On an IFR flight plan in VFR weather, request a top report or a statement that no top report is available, then request to report reaching VFR-on-top.
- Climbing through clouds, haze, or other meteorological formations on an IFR flight plan in VFR conditions, request a top report, a statement that no top report is available, and report reaching VFR-on-top. ATC may include a clearance limit, routing, or an alternative clearance.
- Climbing or descending in VFR conditions on an IFR flight plan.
- ATC must authorize VFR-on-top if requested or if it results in noise abatement benefits.

The rule is in AIM §4-4-8 and JO 7110.65 §12-1-3. Always request VFR-on-top directly from ATC and be ready to provide a top report or a statement that no top report is available.

The instrument currency requirements for IFR operations are in 14 CFR §61.57. Here’s the summary:

- General Requirement: A pilot must complete an IPC within 6 months if they haven't met the IFR experience requirements for more than 6 months.
- IPC: Must cover the areas in the applicable Airman Certification Standards, as detailed in Appendix A of Part 61.
- Conduct: In an appropriate aircraft category; for non-glider operations, a full flight simulator or flight training device can be used; for glider operations, a single-engine airplane or glider is required.
- IPC Conduct: Given by an examiner or a U.S. Armed Forces authorized person, provided the testee is a member of the U.S. Armed Forces.

The full text is in 14 CFR §61.57. For more details, refer to the Airman Certification Standards for your specific rating.

You can descend below the MDA or DA only if you can make a normal rate of descent and land on the intended runway using normal maneuvers. The rule is 14 CFR §91.175(c). If you cannot meet these conditions, execute a missed approach. The AIM's §5-4-7 provides more detail on remaining within the circling approach protected area and ensuring obstacle clearance. Always be prepared to execute a missed approach.

No — you cannot cancel an IFR clearance while in IMC. The rule is in 14 CFR §91.155, which states you must cancel the IFR flight plan when you can operate under VFR conditions. This means being clear of clouds and meeting visibility requirements. Once you meet these conditions, you can cancel the IFR clearance and operate under VFR. For more detail, see AIM 5-1-15.
